MGDA-Decoupled: Geometry-Aware Multi-Objective Optimisation for DPO-based LLM Alignment

Andor Vári-Kakas Affiliation: Prescient Design, CS CoE, Genentech | Roche    Ji Won Park Affiliation: Prescient Design, CS CoE, Genentech | Roche    Natasa Tagasovska Affiliation: Prescient Design, CS CoE, Genentech | Roche
Abstract

Aligning large language models (LLMs) to desirable human values requires balancing multiple, potentially conflicting objectives such as helpfulness, truthfulness, and harmlessness, which presents a multi-objective optimisation challenge. Most alignment pipelines rely on a fixed scalarisation of these objectives, which can introduce procedural unfairness by systematically under-weighting harder-to-optimise or minority objectives. To promote more equitable trade-offs, we introduce MGDA-Decoupled, a geometry-based multi-objective optimisation algorithm that finds a shared descent direction while explicitly accounting for each objective’s convergence dynamics. In contrast to prior methods that depend on reinforcement learning (e.g., GAPO) or explicit reward models (e.g., MODPO), our approach operates entirely within the lightweight Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) paradigm. Experiments on the UltraFeedback dataset show that geometry-aware methods—and MGDA-Decoupled in particular—achieve the highest win rates against golden responses, both overall and per objective.

1 Introduction

In multi-objective LLM alignment, the goal is to fine-tune a language model to satisfy multiple, often conflicting desiderata. While pretraining optimises a sole objective of next-token prediction, aligned models must simultaneously be helpful, truthful, harmless, honest, instruction following, concise, etc. (Bai et al., 2022). These diverse human needs are typically captured by a preference dataset 𝒟={(x,yw,yl)n}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\left\{(x,y_{w},y_{l})_{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{N}, where annotators select a preferred response ywy_{w} over an alternative yly_{l} for a given query xx (Christiano et al., 2017). Leveraging such data, models are typically fine-tuned using either Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022) or Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023). While RLHF requires training an explicit reward model to guide a reinforcement learning loop, DPO optimises the policy directly on the preference pairs without a separate reward function.

However, representing multiple objectives via a single preference dataset often leads to a collapse of information (Wu et al., 2023). In particular, if the annotator pool is skewed—for example, if a majority prioritises helpfulness while a minority prioritises harmlessness—the resulting “aligned” model will inherently reflect these biases, raising major fairness concerns (Casper et al., 2023). To prevent this, recent approaches advocate for maintaining one preference dataset per objective (Chakraborty et al., 2024). This decomposition provides the distinct signals necessary for fine-tuning algorithms to explicitly manage trade-offs, enabling all objectives to be fairly considered rather than being implicitly weighted by dataset demographics (Sorensen et al., 2024).

Problem setup.

We consider a setup with kk distinct objectives, represented by individual pairwise preference datasets 𝒟1,…,𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{k}. Our goal is to design a fine-tuning algorithm that yields a model aligned well across all kk objectives, evaluated on held-out prompts via an AI judge (Zheng et al., 2023). Motivated by real-world scenarios, we focus strictly on lightweight algorithms that operate without the computational overhead of reinforcement learning (Li et al., 2025, e.g., GAPO;), training auxiliary reward models (Zhou et al., 2024, MODPO;), or tuning sensitive hyper-parameters (Agnihotri et al., 2025, MOPO;). Specifically, we find that methods which combine gradients from multiple per-objective DPO instances provide an efficient and effective solution. See Figure 1 for an overview of the framework.

Formally, let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote the trainable policy parametrised by weights θ\theta, and πref\pi_{\text{ref}} be the frozen reference model (e.g., from pretraining). We define the DPO loss (Rafailov et al., 2023) for objective ii as:

ℒi≔−𝔼(x,yw,yl)∼𝒟i​[log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(yw∣x)πref​(yw∣x)−β​log⁡πθ​(yl∣x)πref​(yl∣x))],\mathcal{L}_{i}\coloneqq-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}}\left[\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{w}\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{l}\mid x)}\right)\right]\,,

where σ\sigma is the sigmoid function and β\beta controls the deviation from πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Essentially, the optimisation goal is to simultaneously minimise the losses ℒ1,…,ℒk\mathcal{L}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{L}_{k}.

Challenges and Ideas.

This formulation constitutes a multi-objective optimisation (MOO) problem. The primary challenge is that alignment objectives are often conflicting (e.g., Helpfulness vs. Harmlessness). A standard approach is to optimise a fixed scalarisation ∑i=1kci​ℒi\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}\mathcal{L}_{i} with ∑i=1kci=1\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}=1, but this method has critical limitations. First, fixed scalarisation restricts the solution to the convex hull of the Pareto front, making balanced solutions in non-convex regions inaccessible (Sener and Koltun, 2018). Second, determining suitable coefficients cic_{i} a priori is difficult, and suboptimal weighting often causes the optimiser to over-prioritise easier objectives while neglecting harder ones (Chen et al., 2018). Furthermore, even with suitable coefficients, Yu et al. (2020) demonstrate that the composite landscape formed by summing the objectives can cause standard optimisers like Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) to stall or converge to a suboptimal point far from the Pareto front (surprisingly, even in scenarios where a joint optimum for all objectives is attainable).

To resolve these issues, dynamic scalarisation methods adapt the coefficients during training based on real-time loss or gradient information (see Chen et al. 2025 for a recent extensive summary). A particularly promising direction is the family of algorithms rooted in the Multiple Gradient Descent Algorithm (Désidéri, 2014, MGDA;), which has demonstrated strong theoretical guarantees in multi-task learning (Sener and Koltun, 2018) and empirical success in RLHF (Li et al., 2025). By leveraging the geometry of the gradient landscape, these methods compute a common descent direction that improves all objectives simultaneously, effectively automating the selection of scalarisation coefficients that would otherwise require manual tuning. See Figure 2 for an illustration.

We operationalise alignment as a problem of algorithmic fairness in model capacity allocation. When training policies with preference optimisation, we implicitly decide how to distribute this limited capacity across competing normative desiderata (e.g., Helpfulness, Harmlessness, Honesty). Because these desiderata are typically instantiated through datasets and scoring pipelines that reflect annotator demographics, cultural context, and institutional priorities, common scalarisation choices can enact a form of procedural unfairness—systematically overweighting objectives that are easier to optimise, more represented in data, or more aligned with the base model’s priors. This is especially consequential for downstream agentic systems, where a policy trained under a collapsed objective can repeatedly act in ways that privilege one value regime and reinforce long-run disparities.

To address this, we introduce MGDA-Decoupled, a multi-objective optimisation approach for DPO that computes balancing coefficients from loss-normalised per-objective gradients while applying them to the raw gradients, explicitly managing gradient conflicts and mitigating objective dominance. We evaluate across multiple objectives and models and report both aggregate performance and objective-wise outcomes, emphasising worst-objective behaviour as a fairness-relevant criterion. Overall, our results suggest that fairness-aware alignment need not require expensive RLHF pipelines: multi-objective preference optimisation provides a practical lever for enforcing equitable trade-offs among alignment goals.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose MGDA-Decoupled, a novel algorithm designed to mitigate the scale-sensitivity issues inherent in existing geometry-based methods (Section 2.1).

  • •

    We analyse the failure modes of standard loss- and geometry-based baselines and validate the robustness of MGDA-Decoupled via a controlled optimisation problem (Section 2.2).

  • •

    We empirically evaluate these algorithms on the standard UltraFeedback dataset (Cui et al., 2023), establishing that MGDA-Decoupled consistently achieves the highest overall alignment quality (Sections 3 and 4).

2 Algorithms

In what follows, we introduce the specific algorithms used in our comparison. As illustrated in Figure 1, all methods share the same underlying structure: at each step, they aggregate the per-objective gradients ∇ℒi\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i} into a single update vector ∑i=1kci∇ℒi\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}. The methods differ solely in how they calculate the mixing coefficients cic_{i}.

The most straightforward algorithm, which we refer to as Uniform, employs fixed uniform scalarisation, setting ci≔1/kc_{i}\coloneqq 1/k for all objectives11 1 While specific applications might necessitate non-uniform weighting (e.g., prioritising safety), we employ uniform scalarisation as a neutral baseline, reflecting that our per-objective datasets originate from a common source with identical prompt distributions and no intrinsic hierarchy. throughout training.

We next consider GroupDRO (Sagawa et al., 2019), which dynamically upweights objectives with higher losses to focus on the worst-case performance. It employs a multiplicative update rule based on the exponential of the per-objective losses, allowing for a smooth transition between steps:

ci(t+1)≔ci(t)⋅eη​ℒi∑j=1kcj(t)⋅eη​ℒj,c_{i}^{(t+1)}\coloneqq\frac{c_{i}^{(t)}\cdot e^{\eta\mathcal{L}_{i}}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j}^{(t)}\cdot e^{\eta\mathcal{L}_{j}}}\,, (1)

where η\eta is a hyperparameter governing the sensitivity to loss differences and tt denotes the iteration step. While GroupDRO is dynamic, it remains agnostic to the geometric alignment of gradients.

2.1 MGDA variants

In contrast, MGDA variants explicitly address gradient conflicts by leveraging the geometry of the optimisation landscape (see Figure 2). The original MGDA (Désidéri, 2014) determines the coefficients by finding the minimum-norm vector on the convex hull of the gradients:

arg​minc1,…,ck≥0‖∑i=1kci∇ℒi‖s.t.∑i=1kci=1.\argmin_{c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}\geq 0}\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}=1\,. (2)

Intuitively, the primal problem in Equation 2 is the dual formulation of finding a common descent direction dd that maximizes the worst-case improvement across all objectives:

maxd:‖d‖≤1mini=1k⟨−∇ℒi,d⟩.\max_{d:\|d\|\leq 1}\min_{i=1}^{k}\langle-\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i},d\rangle\,. (3)

However, standard MGDA is highly sensitive to gradient magnitudes, often over-prioritising objectives with small gradient norms (Liu et al., 2021; Sener and Koltun, 2018). To address this, various rescaling strategies have been proposed. A common approach in recent literature, which was adopted by GAPO (Li et al., 2025) for RLHF, is to normalise per-objective gradients to unit length. We refer to this variant as MGDA-Normalised. It computes coefficients ci′c^{\prime}_{i} by solving:

arg​minc1′,…,ck′≥0⁡‖∑i=1kci′​∇ℒi‖∇ℒi‖‖s.t.∑i=1kci′=1,\argmin_{c^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,c^{\prime}_{k}\geq 0}\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{k}c^{\prime}_{i}\frac{\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}}{\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert}\right\rVert\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{k}c^{\prime}_{i}=1\,, (4)

and applies the re-scaled coefficients ci≔ci′/‖∇ℒi‖c_{i}\coloneqq c^{\prime}_{i}/\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert to the raw gradients. While MGDA-Normalised prevents bias towards small gradients, it discards magnitude information entirely, treating converged and un-converged objectives identically.

To address this, we propose MGDA-Decoupled. This method decouples the coefficient calculation from the gradient aggregation: it computes mixing coefficients based on loss-normalised gradients but applies them to the raw gradients. Formally, we solve:

arg​minc1,…,ck≥0⁡‖∑i=1kci​∇ℒiℒi‖s.t.∑i=1kci=1.\argmin_{c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}\geq 0}\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}\frac{\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}}{\mathcal{L}_{i}}\right\rVert\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}=1\,. (5)

2.2 Intuition and toy example

To interpret the effect of normalising by ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} in Equation 5, consider the closed-form solution for the k=2k=2 case where gradients are obtuse. The coefficients are given by:

c1=‖g~2‖2−⟨g~1,g~2⟩‖g~1−g~2‖2andc2=‖g~1‖2−⟨g~1,g~2⟩‖g~1−g~2‖2,c_{1}=\frac{\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{2}\right\rVert^{2}-\langle\tilde{g}_{1},\tilde{g}_{2}\rangle}{\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{1}-\tilde{g}_{2}\right\rVert^{2}}\quad\text{and}\quad c_{2}=\frac{\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{1}\right\rVert^{2}-\langle\tilde{g}_{1},\tilde{g}_{2}\rangle}{\left\lVert\tilde{g}_{1}-\tilde{g}_{2}\right\rVert^{2}}\,, (6)

where g~i≔∇ℒi/ℒi\tilde{g}_{i}\coloneqq\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}/\mathcal{L}_{i}. We observe that the objective with the smaller gradient-to-loss ratio ‖∇ℒi‖/ℒi\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert/\mathcal{L}_{i} receives a larger coefficient. Notably, the inverse ratio ℒi/‖∇ℒi‖\mathcal{L}_{i}/\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert corresponds to the step length derived from the Polyak step size (Polyak, 1987)22 2 The Polyak step size is strictly defined as α=(ℒi−ℒi∗)/‖∇ℒi‖2\alpha=(\mathcal{L}_{i}-\mathcal{L}_{i}^{*})/\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert^{2}. Assuming ℒi∗≈0\mathcal{L}_{i}^{*}\approx 0, the magnitude of the resulting update is ‖α∇ℒi‖=ℒi/‖∇ℒi‖\left\lVert\alpha\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert=\mathcal{L}_{i}/\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert., serving as a first-order proxy for the distance to the optimum (Lemaréchal, 2006). Since Equation 5 naturally assigns higher coefficients to input vectors with smaller norms, MGDA-Decoupled implicitly prioritises objectives estimated to be geometrically further from convergence.

Figure 3 illustrates the behaviour of all algorithms outlined in this section on a 2D toy problem (inspired by Figure 1 of Yu et al. 2020), where two objectives share a global optimum at θ∗=(0,1)\theta^{*}=(0,1), but exhibit drastically different curvature. While ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} is a simple quadratic potential, ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} presents a steep exponential valley along the unit circle. Despite similar initial loss values, the gradient magnitude of ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} is vastly larger, dominating the optimisation landscape. Both Uniform and GroupDRO succumb to this scale imbalance, following the steep gradient of ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} directly to the unit circle boundary before slowly traversing the manifold towards θ∗\theta^{*}. Standard MGDA fails completely: upon reaching the ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} minimum (the unit circle), ‖∇ℒ2‖\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{2}\| vanishes while ‖∇ℒ1‖\|\nabla\mathcal{L}_{1}\| remains large. To minimise the combined gradient norm, MGDA overwhelmingly weights the satisfied objective (ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2}), effectively stalling the optimisation. While MGDA-Normalised removes the gradient magnitude bias, it discards scale information, treating the nearly-solved ℒ2\mathcal{L}_{2} as equally urgent to the high-loss ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1}. This forces an initial detour to the boundary, where the normalised ∇ℒ2\nabla\mathcal{L}_{2} necessitates wasteful zig-zag corrections, slowing down the tangential momentum towards the optimum. In contrast, MGDA-Decoupled leverages the gradient-to-loss ratio as a proxy for distance to optimality. By recognising that ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} has smaller gradient magnitude relative to its remaining loss, it assigns higher weight to ∇ℒ1\nabla\mathcal{L}_{1}, preventing the local steepness of ∇ℒ2\nabla\mathcal{L}_{2} from dictating the optimisation trajectory. This allows MGDA-Decoupled to reach the shared optimum faster than the other algorithms.

3 Experiments

Models.

We evaluate our methods on two state-of-the-art small language models: Gemma-2-2b-it (Rivière et al., 2024), a 2.6B-parameter model trained via knowledge distillation, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025), a 0.5B-parameter model trained on an 18-trillion-token corpus. Both models are initialised from their official instruction-finetuned checkpoints. As these models represent instruction-finetuned reference points, we apply DPO directly without an additional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage.

Datasets.

We utilise the UltraFeedback dataset (Cui et al., 2023), consisting of 6464k prompts, which we split into training (4949k) and test (1515k) sets. Each sample contains a prompt and four model responses, rated on a scale of 11–55 across four objectives: Helpfulness, Instruction Following, Honesty, and Truthfulness. To enable DPO training, we construct objective-specific pairwise preference datasets 𝒟1,…,𝒟4\mathcal{D}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{D}_{4} by evaluating all (42)=6\binom{4}{2}=6 response pairs per prompt. For a given objective, a pair is retained only if the scores differ, establishing a clear preference ordering.

Baselines.

We compare the algorithms outlined in Section 2 (Uniform, GroupDRO, MGDA-Normalised, MGDA-Decoupled) against two baselines. First, Reference, the unmodified starting checkpoint, which serves as an SFT baseline. Second, CDPO, a baseline derived from the no-control variant of Guo et al. (2024). This method collapses the multi-objective structure of the dataset by summing the scores across all four attributes to calculate a single cumulative score for each response. Preference pairs are then constructed based on this total score, reducing the problem to standard single-objective DPO.

Training details.

We train for 11 epoch, with the total number of steps determined by the largest per-objective dataset. Smaller datasets are oversampled to ensure that a valid minibatch is available for every objective at each step. We perform full-parameter fine-tuning using the Adam optimiser (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with a learning rate of 5​e-​75\text{e-}7 and no weight decay. Regarding loss formulation, we set the DPO KL-penalty coefficient to β=0.5\beta=0.5, which we found necessary to mitigate instability observed at lower values. For GroupDRO, we employ a step size of η=0.1\eta=0.1. Comprehensive hyperparameter settings are detailed in Section A.1.

Evaluation details.

We evaluate model performance using the LLM-as-a-judge framework (Zheng et al., 2023) with GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024). For each test prompt, we identify a golden response from the UltraFeedback pool, defined as the response with the highest cumulative score across all four objectives. We then sample responses from our fine-tuned models and conduct pairwise comparisons against these golden responses. The judge evaluates both overall quality and per-objective performance, outputting a win, tie, or loss. We report the Net Win Rate (Win % −- Loss %) following Ning et al. (2023), and use paired bootstrap resampling (Koehn, 2004) with α=0.05\alpha=0.05 to test for significant improvements over the Reference baseline. Evaluation prompts and further details are provided in Section A.2.

Our implementation builds on the open-source repository of Yang et al. (2024a)33 3 https://github.com/SteveKGYang/MetaAligner.

4 Results and Discussion

We present the experimental results for the Gemma-2-2b-it and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct models. We focus on two key dimensions: per-objective performance, measured by the win/tie/loss rate against the golden responses, and overall quality, measured by the improvement in net win rate over the starting Reference model.

Detailed tabular results are provided in Section A.3, and sample responses from the resulting models can be found in Section A.4.

Gemma-2-2b-it

Table 1 details the per-objective performance. MGDA-Decoupled achieves the highest net win rate against the golden responses in three out of four objectives (Instruction Following, Helpfulness, and Truthfulness). In Honesty, where GroupDRO performs the best, we observe a high tie rate (≈47%\approx 47\%). We attribute this to Honesty being effectively binary and many creative prompts lacking factual claims to verify. Figure 4 demonstrates that when evaluated on overall quality, MGDA-Decoupled is the only algorithm to achieve a statistically significant improvement (+2.3%+2.3\%) in net win rate over the Reference policy.

Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct

The results for Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Table 2 and Figure 5) present a more nuanced picture. While MGDA-Normalised has slightly higher net win rates on 3 out of 4 objectives, MGDA-Decoupled shows the highest improvement in overall quality (+4.7%+4.7\% vs +4.1%+4.1\%). In contrast to Gemma-2-2b-it, all fine-tuning algorithms on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct achieved statistically significant gains over Reference.

Discussion

In multi-objective optimisation, it is useful to distinguish between optimisation efficiency (moving closer to the true Pareto front), addressed by a posteriori methods, and optimisation preference (moving along the front to a specific trade-off), addressed by a priori methods (Deb, 2011). The strict dominance of MGDA-Decoupled over Uniform across all objectives with both models suggests that MGDA-Decoupled achieves a solution closer to the Pareto front.

In contrast, the trade-off profile observed, for example, between MGDA-Decoupled and MGDA-Normalised on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (where each method wins on a different set of objectives) indicates that they gravitate towards distinct non-dominated stationary points on the Pareto front. Since neither method uses explicit preference vectors, these trade-offs are inherent to the algorithms. It is worth noting that the performance gains over Reference are relatively small in absolute terms, because the starting models are already high-performing and instruction-finetuned, leaving limited headroom for alignment gains without degrading general capabilities.

A key factor underpinning the success of MGDA-Decoupled in this domain is the homogeneity of the objective functions. Unlike general multi-task learning, where losses may have arbitrary units (e.g., MSE vs. Cross-Entropy) and span drastically different ranges, each objective in our setup uses the identical DPO formulation. Consequently, the loss values serve as a calibrated proxy for optimisation difficulty, where a higher loss ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} indicates a task further from convergence. While MGDA-Normalised discards information from the loss ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} as well as information from the gradient magnitude ‖∇ℒi‖\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert via normalization (Equation 4), MGDA-Decoupled actively preserves and uses those through the ratio ‖∇ℒi‖/ℒi\left\lVert\nabla\mathcal{L}_{i}\right\rVert/\mathcal{L}_{i} (Equation 5), a strategy that proves beneficial within the uniform loss landscape.

The utility of such geometry-aware algorithms is intrinsically linked to the density of gradient conflicts between objectives. While UltraFeedback contains four distinct objectives, some of them can be more correlated than conflicting on certain prompts (e.g., Honesty vs. Truthfulness). Geometric gains would likely be more pronounced in settings involving more numerous or fundamentally opposing objectives (e.g., Helpfulness vs. Harmlessness (Bai et al., 2022)). However, we note that the conservative formulation of DPO itself can dampen these conflicts: the KL-divergence term acts as a shared pull towards the reference model, artificially aligning gradients, particularly when the penalty coefficient β\beta is large.

The UltraFeedback dataset represents a specific, somewhat constrained instance of the general pipeline shown in Figure 1, also shaping our results. First, all per-objective datasets 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} originate from the same prompt-response pool, with samples simply re-paired according to objective-specific scores. As a result, there is substantial overlap across per-objective datasets, which may reduce the density of gradient conflicts. Second, while the original UltraFeedback data provides granular 1–5 scores, the standard DPO reduction discards these in favour of preference pairs. This may lose valuable signal regarding the relative magnitude of improvements. Future work could investigate whether moving beyond the pairwise DPO framework to leverage these raw numerical scores directly would provide a richer signal for multi-objective optimisation.

Finally, we note that MGDA variants introduce a computational overhead from computing the gradient Gram matrix needed for solving the resulting quadratic program (Sener and Koltun, 2018). In our experiments with k=4k=4 objectives, this cost was negligible relative to the forward-backward pass. While the complexity scales quadratically with kk, these algorithms remain feasible for the range of objectives typical in LLM alignment.

5 Related Work

In the context of RLHF, balancing conflicting objectives has traditionally relied on training separate reward models for each objective, which are then combined via fixed linear scalarisation (Wu et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2022). Recognising the limitations of static weighting, recent works have proposed dynamic scalarisation strategies; for instance, Li et al. (2024) employ GroupDRO (Sagawa et al., 2019) to prioritise the worst-performing objective. The algorithm most relevant to our work is GAPO (Li et al., 2025), which is based on the same idea as MGDA-Normalised. However, these methods operate within the reinforcement learning framework, inheriting the instability of Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and high computational overhead—limitations we aim to circumvent by adapting these geometric insights to the lightweight DPO setting.

The efficiency of DPO has spurred a surge of variants aiming to improve preference learning stability (Zhao et al., 2025). In the multi-objective domain, MODPO (Zhou et al., 2024) offers a natural generalisation by scalarising objectives; however, it compromises DPO’s efficiency by requiring the training of explicit reward models. Other approaches reformulate the problem as constrained optimisation (Kim et al., 2025) or controllable generation (Guo et al., 2024) to enforce secondary objectives. Closest to our work is AMoPO (Liu et al., 2025), which shares our goal of an efficient, reward-model-free framework, but balances objectives using generation confidence metrics rather than gradient geometry.

A parallel line of research focuses on steerability, aiming to learn a set of policies or a single conditional policy that is capable of covering relevant regions of the objective space to suit diverse user preferences (Zhong et al., 2024; Gupta et al., 2025). These methods typically rely on inference-time prompts or vectors to modulate model behaviour (Yang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024). Other approaches include model averaging, where models trained on separate objectives are fused in weight space (Ramé et al., 2023). Similarly, Lin et al. (2024) propose interpolating the fine-tuned model with the reference model to mitigate the “alignment tax” (Askell et al., 2021), or the degradation of general capabilities that alignment methods may introduce.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced MGDA-Decoupled, a novel geometry-aware algorithm for multi-objective LLM alignment designed to ensure simultaneous improvement across all objectives while remaining sensitive to their respective convergence dynamics. We systematically evaluated our proposed algorithm against other lightweight, reward-model-free algorithms and benchmarked strategies with varying levels of adaptivity, from fixed linear scalarisation to dynamic schemes based on loss values and gradient geometry.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Training hyperparameters

The hyperparameters used in fine-tuning for all algorithms are enumerated in Table 3. The quadratic programs Equation 4 and Equation 5 were solved iteratively using the Frank-Wolfe method [Sener and Koltun, 2018]. As Gemma-2-2b-it and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct were already instruction-finetuned, we used their official chat templates.

A.2 Evaluation hyperparameters

Table 4 lists the hyperparameters used during inference and evaluation for all algorithms.

A.2.1 LLM-as-a-Judge Prompts

We utilised GPT-4o as a zero-shot pairwise judge. The model received a system prompt establishing its role and strict output format, followed by a user prompt containing the query and two anonymised responses (the model generation and the golden response, presented in randomised order).

The common system prompt was:

⬇
You are an impartial AI judge. Your task is to compare two responses and determine which is better. Return ‘1’ if the first response is better, ‘2’ if the second response is better, or ‘0’ for a tie. You must only return 1, 2, or 0, nothing else.

For overall quality comparisons, the user prompt was:

⬇
QUERY: {query}
RESPONSE 1: {response_1}
RESPONSE 2: {response_2}
Which response is better overall?

For objective-specific comparisons, the final question was adjusted according to the objective:

⬇
QUERY: {query}
RESPONSE 1: {response_1}
RESPONSE 2: {response_2}
Which response is better specifically for the following
criterion: {obj_description}?

The obj_description placeholder was populated using the definitions of the objective, following Yang et al. [2024a]:

  • •

    Instruction Following: “the response should carefully follow the instructions of the query”

  • •

    Honesty: “the response should not tell lies or be deceptive”

  • •

    Helpfulness: “the response should provide useful suggestions and resources to the user”

  • •

    Truthfulness: “the response should actively reveal the full truth of a matter”

A.3 Further results

Example 2

Prompt: Was the Lindbergh kidnapping ever solved?

MGDA-Decoupled:

The Lindbergh kidnapping, which took place in 1932, was officially considered solved in 1936 when Bruno Hauptmann was found guilty of the crime.

Here’s a breakdown:

  • •

    The Crime: Charles Lindbergh Jr., son of the famous aviator Charles Lindbergh, was kidnapped from his crib in New Jersey. The crime sent shockwaves through the nation and became a major media sensation.

  • •

    The Investigation: Extensive efforts were made to find the kidnapper, leading to numerous suspects and investigations. The FBI played a significant role, but progress was slow.

  • •

    The Arrest: Bruno Hauptmann, a German-born carpenter, was arrested in 1935 based on circumstantial evidence, including a ransom note that matched Hauptmann’s handwriting and the discovery of a rifle that he was suspected of owning.

  • •

    The Trial & Conviction: Hauptmann’s trial was highly publicized and led to a controversial conviction. He was eventually executed for the crime in 1936.

  • •

    Controversy and Debate: Despite Hauptmann’s conviction, there have always been those who question the reliability of the evidence and the circumstances surrounding the case. Some argue that the investigation was flawed, and there are still many unanswered questions about what really happened.

In Summary: While the Lindbergh kidnapping remains one of America’s most famous unsolved mysteries, the case was ultimately solved with Bruno Hauptmann’s arrest and conviction. However, lingering questions and controversies continue to fuel debate and fascination with the event.
